title: Causal Separation, Conditional Risk, and Projected Markowitz Portfolios

p.t: Mean-variance portfolio choice [15] is exactly solvable and notoriously fragile: the plug-in solution amplifies estimation error in the mean and in the inverse covariance, to the point that equal weighting is hard to beat out of sample [17,1,4,12]. The standard responses regularize the covariance, through shrinkage [14], norm constraints [9], or factor structure [3,6], and remain agnostic about a prior question: conditional on what information should the moments be computed? Any conditioning set defines a mean, a covariance, and hence a portfolio; the sets are not interchangeable out of sample, and nothing in the covariance-regularization literature selects among them. This paper takes the selection question as primitive and answers it with a single structural condition imported from the theory of common causes [24,21]. Fix a declared, finite universe of candidate drivers, and call a subset a separator if, conditional on its realized path through the investment horizon, the asset returns are mutually independent. The condition is Reichenbach's screening-off property: whatever co-moves the assets is attributable to the conditioning set, so that what remains is idiosyncratic by construction. Everything in the paper is derived from this one condition and two regularity assumptions. The contributions are fivefold. First, we formalize causal separation at the level of σ-algebras, with a conditioning window that closes at the investment horizon and a companion requirement that the asset past is itself screened, and we develop the associated selection theory: the optimal approximate separator exists by construction over the declared universe, the minimal sufficient separator is unique as an information set, and every derived object is invariant under separator equivalence and under smooth reparametrization of the driver state, so the theory depends on the information and not on its coordinates. Second, we make the causal semantics of the condition explicit and prove exactly what it does and does not claim: under a stated structural margin the common causes form a separator; observational data identify the realized information of the causes and not the causal labels; causal and correlational separators of equal observational fit are distinguished by interventions on non-parents; and an unexplained common cause leaves a quantifiable floor on the dependence functional, so latent confounding is detected rather than silently absorbed. Third, we derive the exact structure of conditional risk that the condition induces: the return vector factorizes conditionally, an exact tower decomposition over the two conditioning windows yields a diagonal-plus-low-rank covariance at the decision node, and the low-rank block is identified as the matrix of responses to driver innovations, so the decomposition is a theorem rather than a modelling choice. Fourth, we solve the constrained mean-variance problem in the induced geometry in closed form: the solution is classical Markowitz with the information matrix replaced by its projection onto the constraint-compatible subspace, two-fund separation survives, the conditional efficient frontier is a parabola with an explicit potential, the maximal conditional Sharpe ratio obeys a Hansen-Jagannathan bound whose gap to the unconstrained bound is an exact quadratic form in the shadow prices of the constraint geometry, the entire problem is conditioned by the idiosyncratic variance floor, and an exact two-stage solver with cost linear in the number of assets follows from the structure. Fifth, we develop an exact sensitivity theory under approximate separation, with first-order formulas and distribution-free worst-case bounds for the displacement of the solution and of the frontier at a given tolerance, and we validate every claim in a reproducible suite of seven experiments covering structural identities at machine precision, the two-window factorization, the realized conditional frontier, out-of-sample estimation risk, robustness under injected dependence, invariance under an intervention, and computational scaling.

The scope is deliberately static and mathematical. Dynamics, in which the separator and the response maps move and the intertemporal problem acquires hedging demands in the sense of [16], the finite-sample statistical certification of separators in the sense of [29], and the equilibrium consequences of widespread adoption of the resulting optimizers all lie beyond the present paper. No claim is made about real markets: whether good separators exist for liquid universes, at what tolerance and with what survival times, is an empirical question that the mathematics here makes precise but cannot settle. What the paper establishes is the exact content of the separation condition for static portfolio choice and its measurable consequences in controlled environments. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the separation condition, its two conditioning windows, the selection theory of optimal separators, and the causal semantics of the framework, with its soundness, identification and interventional-invariance results. Section 3 derives the conditional factorization, the tower decomposition and the induced covariance structure, together with the geometry of exposures and admissibility. Section 4 develops the projected Markowitz theory, and Section 5 the sensitivity theory under approximate separation. Section 6 reports the seven experiments, and Section 7 concludes. The complete experiment configuration is collected in Section A.

The fragility of plug-in mean-variance portfolios is documented and quantified in [17,1,12,4], and the robust-optimization response to parameter and model uncertainty is developed in [10]. The covariance-regularization literature addresses the same fragility through shrinkage [14], through norm constraints whose implicit shrinkage explains their effectiveness [9], and through factor structure, from the arbitrage-pricing foundations of approximate factor models [3] to highdimensional factor-based covariance estimation [6]. The role of conditioning information in asset pricing is classical [8,7], and the conditional factor literature makes the second moment conditional through instrumented principal components [13] and dynamic conditional correlations [5]. In all of these approaches the conditioning information, or the factor space, is an input: none of them selects the conditioning set, tests it, or attaches invariance guarantees to it, and these are the questions the present paper takes as primitive. On the causal side, the screening-off property of common causes originates with [24] and is developed in the graphical and structural literature [20,21,23]. Invariant causal prediction [22] identifies causal predictors by their stability under interventions, the principle our intervention experiment instantiates in portfolio space; the hardness of conditional-independence testing and the generalised covariance measure are established in [29], and the econometrics of generated regressors in two-stage estimation goes back to [19]. In finance, [18] argues on methodological grounds that factor investing should be grounded in causal rather than associational structure; the present paper can be read as supplying portfolio-level mathematics for that agenda.

The closest line of work is the causal, sensitivity-based portfolio optimization framework of Rodríguez Domínguez. In that framework, drivers of asset and portfolio dynamics are defined and optimally selected through the commonality principle, which identifies the common causal drivers of the constituents as the optimal drivers of the portfolio's diversification dynamics, with the argument resting on Reichenbach's common cause principle; portfolio constituents are embedded in the space of their sensitivities to the common drivers, where hierarchical and geometric methods deliver idiosyncratic and systematic diversification, with asset dynamics modelled by partial differential equations and sensitivities estimated by neural networks and automatic differentiation [25]. The framework is developed in [27] into a general theory of causal portfolio optimization, including the geometry of the common causal manifold, projection methods that preserve idiosyncratic diversification while optimizing systematic diversification in the sensitivity space, and combinatorial methodologies for causal driver selection. Its dynamic side comprises a conditional risk-neutral partial differential equation for the portfolio law given its common causal drivers, supporting dynamic risk management through implied conditional volatilities and weights [26], and, in full generality, causal PDE-control models that couple forward density evolution, backward stochastic control and nonlinear filtering under partial information, grounded in causal invariance principles [28]. The present paper is complementary to this framework and narrower in scope: it isolates the probabilistic condition that underlies conditioning on common causal drivers, takes that condition as the primitive at the level of σ-algebras, and characterizes what it alone delivers for static mean-variance choice, with selection, uniqueness, invariance and robustness guarantees. The sensitivity-based and PDE-control formulations operate in dynamic, generally nonlinear settings under partial information; the static theory developed here is an analysis of the conditioning condition itself, prior to those layers.

A reader will recognize the induced diagonal-plus-low-rank covariance as that of an approximate factor model, and the relation to that literature is best stated as three nested readings, each with its own assumptions. When the factor space is known, the method reduces to structured factorcovariance Markowitz with linear constraints, and in a static linear world the projected solution numerically coincides with the factor-model solution; our experiments confirm the coincidence, and we regard it as evidence that the framework has the correct classical limit. When the driver space is selected rather than given, the contribution is the selection criterion itself, with existence, uniqueness, minimality and invariance guarantees, together with the testability of screening-off as a conditional-independence property of an identified information set rather than an unidentified latent rotation. The causal reading, finally, requires additional structural assumptions or interventional evidence, and the paper states exactly which: under an explicit structural margin the common causes form a separator, observational data identify their realized information and no more, and causal and correlational separators of equal fit are distinguished by interventions on non-parents, a property our experiments measure directly. Nothing in the second reading depends on the third, and nothing in the portfolio theory depends on either.

p.s: The separation condition and its two windows
p.t: Definition 2.4 (Separator; screening-off). Fix t, an estimation window δ > 0, a horizon bound with mutual (not merely pairwise) independence required, together with the further requirement that the asset past is itself screened: Sep t (A; δ, H) denotes the set of separators. Conditions (1)-( 2) are jointly the screening-off property of common causes [24,21]: conditioning on the drivers' realized path through the horizon makes the constituents independent (1), and past returns, being effects of past drivers and past idiosyncratic shocks rather than additional causes, add nothing once that path is given (2). This pair is the only structural condition of the paper.

Screening-off (1) alone gives independence given F D [t-δ,t+h] ; the risk objects of Section 3 condition on the join F A t ∨ F D [t-δ,t+h] , and enlarging a conditioning σ-algebra can destroy conditional independence (past returns are common descendants of the idiosyncratic shocks). (S0) is exactly the hypothesis that closes this gap: it states that the extra conditioning is informationally inert for the horizon return given the realized cause, so the joint conditional law, and with it the product structure, transfers verbatim to the join (Theorem 3.1). The condition costs nothing that the framework needs to keep: µ t = E[r t+h | G t ] may still depend on the asset past, through its ability to forecast the future driver path (under (S0) the conditional mean is E[g(D-path) | G t ] for the closed-window regression function g); what (S0) forbids is a residual, driver-free channel from past returns to future returns, which is precisely what a separator is intended to rule out. It is testable with the same conditional-independence battery as (1) (add lagged returns to the conditioning regressors and test their increment), and it holds identically in the normal form (10), where given the driver path the asset past is a function of past idiosyncratic shocks, independent of the horizon ones. Remark 2.6 (Two windows, two roles). The conditioning window in (1) is closed at the horizon, and this is forced rather than optional: the common cause of the covariation of horizon-h returns is the driver path through t + h, and in any model in which returns load on contemporaneous driver innovations, no past σ-algebra can screen those innovations off. Reichenbach's principle conditions on the value of the cause, and the realized cause is the closed-window path. The two windows then play strictly separate roles: the δ-lookback carries the memory of the response maps; the horizon extension carries the common innovations. The decision σ-algebra G t of Theorem 2.11 remains past-only, so that no anticipative information is ever used to choose w t , while the closed window appears exclusively inside the separation property, its statistical tests, and the residual objects they define. Since F D W ⊆ F D ′ W for D ⊆ D ′ under either window W , all lattice and preorder structure below is window-independent. Figure 1 provides the empirical counterpart of this remark.

Fix a dependence functional dep on pairs of conditional laws (maximal residual correlation, the generalized covariance measure of [29], HSIC, or conditional mutual information), normalized so that dep = 0 iff conditional independence holds within the working model class. Define ϵ t (D) := max i<j∈A sup h∈(0,H] and call D an ϵ-separator if ϵ t (D) ≤ ϵ. Theorem 2.8 (Existence of the optimal approximate separator). Under (A1), for every t, A, (δ, H) the value ϵ * t := min D⊆{1,...,M } ϵ t (D) is attained, and among its attainers there is at least one minimal for the sufficiency preorder of Theorem 2.11. Every construction of the paper is carried out at tolerance ϵ * t : exact separation is the boundary case ϵ * t = 0, and the deviation ϵ * t > 0 is a quantity that enters the theory explicitly (Section 5), never an assumption. Proof. The lattice of subsets is finite, so the minimum is attained; restricting the preorder to the finite attainment set gives a minimal element, since every finite preordered set has one. Remark 2.9 (Computation and statistical control of the selection). Exhaustive search over the 2 M subsets is feasible only for small declared universes. Three practical devices cover the general case, at the cost of guarantees that are stated rather than hidden. First, forward selection with backward elimination: grow the candidate greedily by the largest decrease of εt , then prune any element whose removal does not increase it, at a cost of O(M 2 ) fits; the forward stage alone can be misled by informative proxies of true causes, and the backward stage is what restores minimality, a phenomenon the lattice of our intervention experiment displays explicitly. Second, a penalized criterion εt (D) + κ|D| with κ > 0 breaks ties among near-attainers in favour of minimal sets and turns the argmin-plus-minimality rule into a single objective. Third, the combinatorial causal-discovery methodologies of [27], including Bayesian-network and correlation-based driver selection, are compatible search engines for the same functional. Statistically, the selected set is a random object and εt evaluated on the selection sample is optimistically biased; the elementary remedy is sample splitting, selecting on one segment and certifying on a disjoint one, under which the certified tolerance retains its nominal interpretation. This is step 3 of the operational workflow of Section 6.1 and the design of the field protocol of Section 6.9; the in-sample values reported in the intervention experiment are labelled as such and serve ranking, not certification. A full post-selection theory, with error control over the lattice and sequentially valid monitoring, is beyond this paper, and the sensitivity results of Section 5 are stated so as to consume whatever certified tolerance such a theory delivers. Remark 2.10 (Status of the common cause principle). Reichenbach's principle therefore enters as motivation rather than as an axiom: the theory nowhere assumes that cross-asset dependence is attributable to observable common causes. It assumes a declared universe and works at the achievable tolerance ϵ * t . The economically substantive claim, that ϵ * t is small for well-chosen universes, is a falsifiable proposition about markets, external to the mathematics, and no statement below is immunized against its failure because every statement carries the tolerance explicitly.

p.s: Causal semantics: soundness, identification, and interventional invariance
p.t: The separation condition of Theorem 2.4 is stated, and is testable, at the purely observational level: it is a conditional-independence property of an identified σ-algebra, and every portfolio-level result of Sections 3 to 5 is a consequence of that property alone. The adjective causal is nevertheless earned, in a precise and limited sense that this subsection makes explicit through three statements: a soundness theorem (causal structure implies separation), an identification proposition (what observational data can and cannot identify), and an interventional invariance theorem (the property that distinguishes a causal separator from an observationally equivalent correlational one, and the one our intervention experiment measures). A fourth statement shows that an unexplained common cause leaves a quantifiable floor on the dependence functional, so that latent confounding is detected rather than silently absorbed.

There is a structural causal model over the window [t -δ, t + H] whose variables include the driver values {D k s }, the returns {r i s }, and mutually independent exogenous noises, such that: (i) the joint law is Markov with respect to the associated acyclic graph; (ii) returns are sink nodes: within the window, no return is a cause of any other return, of any driver, or of any other variable (no contagion channel among assets and no feedback from returns to drivers at the horizon of the decision); (iii) the exogenous noise entering each return is specific to that asset and date; (iv) every variable that is a common cause of two or more assets' returns within the window has its window path measurable with respect to F C [t-δ,t+h] for a subset C ⊆ {1, . . . , M } of the declared universe; (v) every variable in C is an ancestor of the returns or exogenous: no declared driver in C is a common effect of variables outside C. Part (ii) is the substantive economic content: it excludes direct cross-asset causation (for example, fire-sale contagion operating inside the horizon) except insofar as such channels are themselves represented by declared drivers; part (iv) says the universe is rich enough to observe the common causes; part (v) excludes collider conditioning, and its practical reading is a warning: an index constructed by aggregating asset-specific causes, and in particular any driver derived from the assets themselves, is a dangerous conditioner, since conditioning on a common effect manufactures dependence between its causes. Neither faithfulness nor linearity is assumed. Proposition 2.17 (Soundness: causal structure implies separation). Under (A4), the set C of (A4)(iv) satisfies (1) and (2): C ∈ Sep t (A; δ, H).

Proof. Fix h and condition on F A t ∨ F C [t-δ,t+h] . By the Markov property it suffices to show that r i t+h and r j t+h are d-separated given the conditioning set, and that r t+h is d-separated from the past returns given F C [t-δ,t+h] . Every edge into r i t+h comes either from a driver-side variable or from its own exogenous noise, by (A4)(ii)-(iii). Any path connecting r i t+h to another return therefore leaves r i t+h through one of these parents. If it leaves through a driver-side parent, the path either passes through a common-cause variable, which is blocked because its window path is in the conditioning set by (A4)(iv), or reaches the other return only through such a variable, with the same conclusion; and no conditioned variable acts as a collider on any path, by (A4)(v). If it leaves through the exogenous noise of asset i at t + h, the path terminates: that noise has a single child by (A4)(iii) and no other connections. Conditioning on past returns opens collider paths at those returns, but any such opened path connects past exogenous noises and driver-side variables among themselves; to reach r i t+h it must still enter through a blocked driver-side parent or through the terminal noise, so no new connection to the horizon returns is created. The same blocking argument run without conditioning on the past returns, where no collider is opened at all, gives mutual independence given F C [t-δ,t+h] alone, which is (1); the argument between r t+h and F A t on the join gives (2). Note the order: (1) is not deduced from the joint statement by shrinking the conditioning σ-algebra, which would be illegitimate, but by rerunning the separation argument at each conditioning level. Proposition 2.18 (Identification: information, not labels). Separators are identified from observational data at most up to their generated closed-window σ-algebras. In particular: (i) if S is any observable process with F S [t-δ,t+h] = F D [t-δ,t+h] for a separator D and all h, then S is a separator, whether or not S is a cause of anything; a noiseless, invertible recording of the true common causes is the canonical example. (ii) Consequently, no observational criterion, the dependence functional (3) included, can distinguish a mechanism from an exact measurement of it: causal parenthood of the declared labels is not identified by screening-off alone.

Proof. Every object in Theorems 2.4 and 2.7 is a functional of conditional laws given the generated σ-algebras; equal σ-algebras give equal conditional laws, which proves (i), and (ii) is (i) applied to an injective bimeasurable transformation of the causes. Theorem 2.18 delimits the claim rather than weakening it: what screening-off identifies is the realized information of the common causes, which is exactly the object the portfolio theory consumes, by the invariance results of Theorem 2.15. Distinguishing a cause from an observationally equivalent proxy of it requires leaving the observational distribution, which is the content of the next statement and the reason interventions, not fit, are the arbiter. Theorem 2.19 (Interventional invariance: the causal certificate). Assume (A4) and let C be as in Theorem 2.17. Consider any intervention that replaces the structural assignments of a set V of variables having no directed path into any return within the window (non-ancestors of the assets). Then: (i) the joint interventional law of the returns and of the window paths of the variables in (A4)(iv) coincides with the observational one; consequently C remains a separator with the same ϵ t (C), and every derived object, the conditional mean, Q, w * and ∆ t , is unchanged. (ii) By contrast, in the linear normal form (10) augmented with a proxy P := Z 1 + τ u, u independent noise, consider the candidate D ′ = {P, Z 2 }, whose screening of the Z 1 -channel operates entirely through the observational assignment of P . After an intervention that replaces that assignment by independent noise with the same marginal law, the conditional residual variance of the Z 1 innovations given F D ′ rises from λ = Λ 11 τ 2 /(Λ 11 + τ 2 ) to λ = Λ 11 , and ϵ t (D ′ ) is bounded below by the dependence floor (6) evaluated at the full innovation variance.

Proof. (i) By the truncated factorization of the intervened model, the law of any set of variables that are non-descendants of V is unchanged; returns and the common-cause paths are non-descendants of V since V contains no ancestor of the returns and the graph is acyclic. All quantities named are functionals of that joint law. (ii) After the intervention P is independent of Z 1 , so conditioning on (P, Z 2 ) leaves the Z 1 innovation entirely unexplained; Theorem 2.20 applies with λ = Λ 11 . The pre-intervention value of λ is the conditional variance of the Z 1 innovation given the proxy, namely Λ 11 -Λ 2 11 /(Λ 11 + τ 2 ) = Λ 11 τ 2 /(Λ 11 + τ 2 ) by Gaussian projection. Proposition 2.20 (Dependence floor of an unexplained common cause). In the linear normal form (10), let a factor with loadings b ∈ R n have, conditionally on the σ-algebra used for screening, residual innovation variance λ > 0, and let b i b j ̸ = 0 for some pair. Then the conditional correlation of the residuals of assets i and j is exactly so that ϵ t (D) ≥ max i<j |ρ ij | > 0 for every candidate D that leaves the factor unexplained. Two consequences: a common cause excluded from the declared universe places a floor on the attainable tolerance, so latent confounding is detected by the certificate rather than absorbed into a false separation; and an intervention that destroys a proxy's informativeness about a cause raises the proxy model's dependence functional to the same floor, which is the mechanism of Theorem 2.19(ii).

Proof. Conditionally, the residual of asset i is b i ξ + ς i ζ i with ξ the unexplained factor innovation, Var ξ = λ, and ζ idiosyncratic; (6) is the resulting correlation, and the bound on ϵ t is an equality of functional values when dep is the maximal absolute residual correlation, the working choice of Section 5; for other admissible functionals of Theorem 2.7 the statement holds with the corresponding value of (6) under that functional's normalization.

p.s: Remark 2.21 (When the word causal is earned).
p.t: The framework therefore operates at three stated levels, and the terminology tracks them. At the observational level, separation is testable screening-off; all of Sections 3 to 5 holds at this level with no causal input, and a reader who prefers may read "separator" as a purely statistical object throughout those sections. At the structural level, under (A4) the common causes form a separator (Theorem 2.17) and observational data identify their realized information (Theorem 2.18). At the interventional level, causal and correlational separators that are observationally comparable are distinguished by Theorem 2.19, whose two halves our intervention experiment measures, and latent confounding is quantitatively detected by Theorem 2.20. The causal claims of the paper are exactly these statements, under exactly these assumptions, and no others. 3 The structure of conditional risk

Proposition 3.5 (The decision-node covariance). p.s: Failure modes and the domain of the assumptions
p.t: The assumptions are strong and their failure modes are part of the theory's honest perimeter. The idiosyncratic floor (A3)(iii) enters every constant: the conditioning bound, the Lipschitz constants and the worst-case sensitivity all scale as ς -2 , so a small floor degrades the guarantees quantitatively and visibly rather than invalidating them; an asset with negligible idiosyncratic variance is, in this framework, an asset whose risk is entirely systematic, and the bounds say precisely that such an asset makes the projected problem as ill-conditioned as the classical one. Near collinearity of driver innovations makes Λ nearly singular; the solution and frontier remain well defined as long as Q ≻ 0, which the floor guarantees, but the identification of individual columns of B degrades, and the two-stage solver should then use a factored or pseudoinverse form of Λ; the gauge invariance results are the formal statement that only the column space, not the coordinates, carries meaning. Heteroskedasticity is accommodated by construction: the diagonal block of the covariance is E[Σ c t | G t ], which may depend on the state, and the floor is required only as a uniform lower bound; conditional-variance dynamics affect the power of correlation-based tests, for which the generalised covariance measure [29] is the appropriate instrument. Heavy tails split into two separate questions: the separation property is a statement about conditional laws and survives without moments, while the mean-variance layer requires conditional second moments, and correlation-based dependence functionals lose validity, so rankbased or kernel-based functionals should replace them in the definition of ϵ t , which Theorem 2.7 permits. Conditional independence throughout means independence of conditional laws; the working dependence functional operationalizes it within a declared test class, and every certificate is relative to that class, a relativity that Theorem 2.7 makes explicit rather than implicit. Finally, the intersection property (A2) fails under exact deterministic redundancy among drivers, for instance a duplicated driver, in which case minimal sufficient separators need not be unique as subsets; they remain equivalent as σ-algebras, which is the invariance the theory actually uses, and the failure is detectable as exact collinearity in the fitted driver dynamics.

Seven experiments are reported: three validate the mathematics (identities at machine precision, the two-window factorization, the realized frontier), four quantify the practical content (estimation risk, robustness, invariance under intervention, computation). All are fully reproducible from the accompanying package with fixed seeds; the complete suite runs in a few minutes on standard hardware.

The data-generating process is the normal form (10): m drivers with persistence Φ = ϕI, ϕ = 0.95 (half-life ≈ 14 days at daily frequency), stationary unit driver variances; loadings B ij ∼ N (0, 0.04 2 ); idiosyncratic volatilities ς i ∼ U [0.8%, 2%] per day; risk premia carried by the state, µ(z) = a + Gz with G = B diag(θ) and θ scaled per experiment. Estimation throughout is the two-stage map of Theorems 3.1 and 3.5: fit the driver dynamics with an intercept, extract innovations η, run the closed-window regression of returns on (1, Z t , ηt+1 ), and assemble Q = B Λ B⊤ + diag(ς 2 ), with the conditional mean â + ĜZ t read from the past block. The operational workflow, executed at each decision date t entirely on information available at t, is the following, and it is the workflow every experiment below implements. 1. Observe the past window of drivers and returns. 2. Fit the driver dynamics with an intercept on the past window and extract the historical innovations ηs for s ≤ t.

Assemble the decision-node inputs μt = â+ ĜZ t and Q = B Λ B⊤ +diag(ς 2 ), both G t -measurable. 5. Solve the projected program with the two-stage solver and trade w * t . No step consumes information beyond t: the horizon-closed window enters only through historical realized triples, in which the innovation at s ≤ t is past data at decision time, exactly as Theorem 2.6 prescribes; the method is operational, not merely diagnostic, and it is free of lookahead by construction. In the experiments the fit of steps 2-3 is refreshed per training block rather than at every date, an implementation choice that only strengthens the no-look-ahead property. Mean-variance portfolios use γ = 0.05 throughout E2; annualization uses 252 days. The complete configuration of every experiment, including dimensions, premium scales, replications and seeds, is collected in Table 5, so the paper is self-contained without the code package. Code availability is concrete: the package accompanying the submission contains the generator, the estimation map, both solvers, the selection routines, one script per experiment and a master script (run all.py) that regenerates every figure and table of this section from fixed seeds in a single run of a few minutes; the environment is pinned (Python 3.12, numpy 2.4.4, scipy 1.17.1, matplotlib 3.10.8), the license is MIT, no experiment uses proprietary data or tuned hyperparameters, and a public repository link will accompany publication.

p.s: E1: the two windows are empirically sharp
p.t: Figure 1 conditions the same simulated panel (n = 30, m = 3, T = 500, 400 replications) two ways. Past-window residuals (returns regressed on Z t alone) carry the full systematic block BΛB ⊤ : the maximal absolute off-diagonal residual correlation is 0.83, and Fisher-z tests reject independence for 82% of pairs at the 5% level. Closed-window residuals (regressed on (Z t , ηt+1 )) show no dependence: maximal off-diagonal correlation 0.025 on a T = 20,000 path, and the rejection rate tracks the nominal level along the 45 • line, with size 4.5% at the 5% level. These results are the empirical counterpart of Theorem 2.6: separation holds exactly where the theory places it, on the horizon-closed algebra, and fails exactly where the theory forbids it, on the past algebra, while every regressor used by the tests is past data at test time. One econometric caveat applies: the conditioning regressors include the estimated innovations η, so the Fisher-z battery operates on generated regressors [19] and its degrees-of-freedom adjustment is not the generated-regressor correction. The observed size indicates that the distortion is negligible in this design, and the generalised covariance measure of [29], constructed to tolerate first-stage estimation at o(T -1/4 ) rates, is a direct replacement where formal guarantees are required.

p.s: E2: estimation risk out of sample
p.t: Table 1 reports the estimation-risk comparison. Global-minimum-variance portfolios are built from seven covariance estimators, namely the sample covariance, Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage [14], principal components with the factor count misspecified low (m -2), correct (m) and misspecified high (m+2), the causal structured Q, and the oracle Q, across n ∈ {50, 100, 200} and T ∈ {126, 252, 504}, with 250 Monte Carlo replications per cell, evaluated on 252 out-of-sample days. Monte Carlo standard errors are below 0.06 percentage points of volatility, excluding the singular cell, and 0.17 of Sharpe. Two designs are reported for the mean-variance rows. Under the static-hold design, weights are computed once, at the signal Z T , and held for the entire out-of-sample year; this is the one-shot deployment that isolates estimation risk from signal dynamics, and since the signal half-life is approximately fourteen days, static Sharpe levels are intentionally modest. Under the daily-rebalanced design, fitted parameters are frozen and weights are recomputed each day at the current state. Because Sharpe levels in either design are artifacts of the simulator's premium scale, Table 2 reports a scale-free quantity: the fraction of the same-policy oracle Sharpe ratio captured, with static estimators normalized by the static oracle, whose level is a realistic 1.1 annualized, and the rebalanced strategy normalized by the rebalanced oracle, whose level of 11.8 at this daily signal strength is a simulator artifact that the ratio removes. The table also reports the mean daily one-way turnover of the rebalanced causal strategy as a fraction of gross exposure.

p.s: E2: estimation risk out of sample
p.t: Four observations follow. First, the sample covariance degrades as n/T grows and fails at n = 200, T = 126, where realized volatility reaches 277%: the training covariance is rank deficient, the associated KKT system is numerically singular, and the solver returns the unstable weights that constitute the documented pathology, the canonical Markowitz failure [17,1,12]. Second, the structured estimator matches the oracle to a few basis points of annualized volatility at every (n, T ), and its calibration remains at 1.03 to 1.04 where the sample covariance reaches 26 and shrinkage 2.5; predicted risk is therefore reliable, which is Theorem 4.5 in operation, and Fig. 2 displays both metrics across n. Third, the classical-limit agreement discussed in Section 1.1 has a converse: principal components with the correct factor count are indistinguishable from the causal estimator, but principal components missing two factors carry 46% more realized risk, 2.13% against 1.46% at n = 200, T = 252, while their calibration of 1.10 understates the misspecification. This failure mode of latent-factor selection is removed by an identified conditioning set, since the causal estimator does not choose a factor count: the drivers are declared observables. Fourth, regarding the mean, the sample-mean plug-in captures between 0 and 18% of the attainable static Sharpe ratio, against 39 to 76% for the conditional mean on the selected state, rising with T in both designs. Turnover of the rebalanced strategy is a steady 29% of gross exposure per day at this signal speed, a magnitude at which transaction costs are first order, so no cost-free performance claim is made and the friction-aware treatment is left to future work.

p.s: E5: the sensitivity bounds under injected dependence
p.t: Residual cross-correlation of maximal size ϵ ∈ [0, 0.3] (equicorrelated pattern, the worst rank-one direction) is injected into the residual block and the exact displacement of w * and ∆ is compared with the first-order formulas of Theorem 5.1 and the worst-case bounds of Theorem 5.2 (Fig. 4). The first-order displacement of the potential overlays the actual value, with 8.7 × 10 -4 predicted against 8.9 × 10 -4 realized at ϵ = 0.1. The displacement of the solution shows visible second-order curvature beyond ϵ ≈ 0.1, with 1.16 realized against 1.42 at first order, as the remainder terms permit. For an estimated tolerance of a few percent, the empirically relevant regime, the induced frontier error is second order in practice.

This experiment separates the framework from an equally well-fitting correlational factor model, and it is the one place where the intervention operator appears, so we ground it in an explicit structural causal model with three assignments: Z exogenous with the dynamics of (10); P := Z 1 + τ u with u independent noise (corr(P, Z 1 ) ≈ 0.98); r t+1 := a + GZ t + Bη t+1 + ς ⊙ ζ t+1 . The intervention do(P ) replaces the structural assignment of P by independent noise with the same marginal law and touches nothing else; since P is a non-parent of r, the interventional law of returns equals the observational one, and invariance of any predictor built on the true parents is exactly the identification principle of [22], here instantiated in portfolio space. The experiment is the empirical instantiation of Theorem 2.19: part (i) predicts that the causal separator and every object built on it are unchanged by the intervention, and part (ii), through the dependence floor of Theorem 2.20, predicts the collapse of the proxy model, whose access to the cause Z 1 is destroyed while its marginal fit is preserved. Both models, the true pair {Z 1 , Z 2 } and the proxy pair {P, Z 2 }, are fitted on 750 days and traded with daily rebalancing; the intervention occurs midway through the test period. Figure 5 reports 250 replications. Before the intervention the two portfolios are statistically comparable; the proxy portfolio's Sharpe ratio is in fact slightly higher, at 1.37 against 1.06, so invariance is invisible both in sample and out of sample before the shift, which is why it is easily neglected. After the intervention the causal portfolio does not move, with Sharpe ratio 1.06 to 1.07 and information coefficient of its conditional mean 0.073 to 0.071, while the proxy portfolio's Sharpe ratio collapses to 0.58 and its information coefficient halves, from 0.072 to 0.036, consistent with the loss of one of two channels that are symmetric in expectation under the random loadings of the design: the Z 1 channel of its signal is inactive after the intervention while the Z 2 channel survives. Three further observations complete the experiment. First, the in-sample residual-dependence functional ranks the models before any intervention: the value is 0.12 for the causal separator, of the order of the finite-sample envelope for the maximum of n 2 independent Gaussian correlations, 2 log n 2 /T ≈ 0.13, quoted as an order-of-magnitude reference rather than a critical value since the residuals are estimated and weakly dependent, against 0.69 for the proxy, whose misspecified innovations leave common variation unexplained; the dependence diagnostic detects in the residuals what performance comparisons cannot detect in the returns. Second, the selection principle of Theorem 2.7 and Theorem 2.8 runs end to end on this universe: exhaustive search over all fifteen candidate subsets of {Z 1 , Z 2 , P, W }, where W is a pure-noise decoy, yields the in-sample ranking of Table 4; the four near-attainers of the minimum are exactly the supersets of {Z 1 , Z 2 }, tied at approximately 0.12, with {Z 1 , Z 2 } the minimal element among them, while every proxy-based or noise-based set lies between 0.69 and 0.86, so the minimization-plus-minimality rule of Section 2 selects the causal set from data alone. The same table carries two further messages. Read along the subsets that exclude a true cause, it is Theorem 2.20 in data: every candidate that leaves Z 1 or Z 2 unexplained sits on a dependence floor between 0.69 and 0.86, so latent confounding is detected by the certificate, not silently absorbed into a false separation. Read as a search problem, it illustrates Theorem 2.9: pure forward selection is misled at the first step, picking the proxy P (the best singleton at 0.83 against 0.84 for either true driver), then Z 2 (reaching 0.69), then Z 1 (reaching 0.12), and it is the backward-elimination stage that prunes P at no cost in the functional and returns the minimal set {Z 1 , Z 2 } in O(M fits. Third, trading intensity is comparable across the two models, with mean daily one-way turnover of 24% against 28% of gross exposure, so the post-intervention gap is not a turnover artifact, and no anticipative information is involved anywhere: the intervention is detected through its consequences.

Figure 6: the two-stage solver of Theorem 4.8 against the dense KKT solve, k = 10 drivers, n up to 4000. Solutions agree to 1.3 × 10 -12 uniformly. The dense solver exhibits a measured log-log slope above two, consistent with its entry into the cubic regime, while the two-stage solver's measured slope is well below one; the latter is not a sublinear algorithm, since its theoretical cost is linear in n at fixed k, and the measured exponent below one reflects memory-traffic and BLAS overheads dominating the arithmetic in this range. At n = 4000 the structured solve is roughly three orders of magnitude faster, and it never materializes the n × n covariance, so memory is O(nk); rebalancing a book of several thousand assets at high frequency is computationally feasible within this framework.

p.s: From simulation to field data: a pre-specified evaluation protocol
p.t: The experiments above are synthetic by design, because the paper's claims are mathematical and controlled environments are where mathematical claims are falsifiable. The empirical question they do not and cannot answer, whether good approximate separators exist in actual markets, deserves a pre-specified protocol rather than an afterthought, and the reproducibility package implements one in full (field protocol.py), runnable on any user-supplied panel of returns and candidate drivers. The protocol fixes, before any data are seen: the declared universes, for example equity panels with candidate drivers drawn from traded factor portfolios, sector indices, volatility indices, rates and commodities; currency panels with rates, carry, a dollar factor and volatility; or futures panels with inflation, rates and trend variables; the windowing, with selection and certification on disjoint segments of each rolling window and evaluation strictly out of sample, following the workflow of Section 6.1; and the reported quantities, namely the certified tolerance εt per window with its time series and stability across windows, the selected sets and their survival times, and the same functional evaluated on the residuals of principal-component factor models with matched dimension as the reference. The protocol's outcomes are informative in every direction: small and stable certified tolerances would locate universes where the theory's premise holds, large ones are, by Theorem 2.20, evidence of unobserved common causes and therefore a measurement of what is missing from the declared universe rather than a failure of the method, and instability quantifies the survival-time question directly. No performance claim is attached to the protocol; its object is the certificate, which is the quantity this paper's theory prices.

The paper isolates what a single structural condition delivers in static portfolio choice. The condition, screening-off by a declared driver set with the horizon-closed conditioning window that Theorem 2.6 shows to be forced, yields the diagonal-plus-low-rank conditional covariance as a theorem, the projected Markowitz solution in closed form, a realized conditional frontier, an exact price for the admissibility geometry, regularization by the idiosyncratic floor, invariance under both separator equivalence and reparametrization, an O(nk 2 ) exact solver, and computable sensitivity to the certified tolerance ϵ. The experiments confirm each class of claim at the appropriate resolution: identities at machine precision, statistical properties at nominal levels, and economic magnitudes in realistic ranges. Three developments are deliberately excluded and remain open. The first is dynamics: when the separator, the response maps and the admissible geometry move, the state variable of the intertemporal problem is the manifold itself, and the optimal policy adds to (13) a hedging demand against manifold motion in the sense of [16]. The second is certification: the finite-sample statistics of the estimated tolerance, including test batteries across model classes, error control after selection over the candidate lattice and sequential monitoring, together with a transfer theorem converting a statistical tolerance into the risk bounds of Section 5. The third is equilibrium: the consequences of adoption of the optimizers of Theorem 4.1 by a continuum of agents whose trading feeds back into the drivers.

Two limitations should be stated. The experiments are synthetic by design: the paper's claims are mathematical, and controlled environments are where mathematical claims are testable; whether good separators exist for liquid universes, at what tolerance and with what survival times, is an empirical question rather than a corollary of the theory, and Section 6.9 specifies, and the package implements, the protocol by which it should be answered. The synthetic choice here is deliberate and complementary to the empirical record of the framework it analyzes: the sensitivity-based and PDE-control line of [25,26,27,28] reports extensive implementations on real asset panels and real driver universes, including equity and multi-asset allocations and brokerage-data studies, where the object of interest is out-of-sample portfolio performance. The present paper sets performance aside precisely in order to isolate theoretical validation: in a controlled environment the structural identities, the factorization, the frontier and the invariance claims can be checked exactly and falsifiably against a known data-generating process, which real data cannot provide. The two modes are complementary, empirical evidence of value on one side and exact verification of the mathematics on the other, and the field protocol connects them by carrying the theoretical object, the certified tolerance, to real panels.
